topic: Biostatistics: Sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV made easy

slides.title: Biostats Viva: Sens, Spec, PPV & NPV
slides.subtitle: High-yield formulas, worked examples & pearls for MD/DNB pediatrics

slides.title: Q: Set up the classic 2x2 table?
slides.subtitle: Always keep disease on top, test result on side
points: Disease Present (D+): True Positives (a) + False Negatives (c) = Total (a + c)
Disease Absent (D-): False Positives (b) + True Negatives (d) = Total (b + d)
Test Positive (T+): Sum of row 1 = a + b (used as denominator for PPV)
Test Negative (T-): Sum of row 2 = c + d (used as denominator for NPV)
slides.highlight: Vertical columns = Disease status (Sens/Spec); Horizontal rows = Test outcome (PPV/NPV)

slides.title: SnNOut vs SpPIn
slides.subtitle: How examiners test your clinical application
points: S - Sensitivity looks at True Positive rate [a / (a + c)]
N - Negative test result with high sensitivity
Out - Rules OUT disease reliably (used for screening tests)
S - Specificity looks at True Negative rate [d / (b + d)]
P - Positive test result with high specificity
In - Rules IN disease reliably (used for confirmatory tests)
slides.highlight: High Sensitivity = Low False Negatives. High Specificity = Low False Positives.

slides.title: Q: What is the Prevalence Trap?
slides.subtitle: Crucial distinction between test parameters
points: Sensitivity & Specificity: Stable test characteristics; do NOT change with prevalence
Prevalence increases: PPV rises markedly, NPV drops
Prevalence decreases: PPV plummets (more false positives), NPV approaches 100%
Clinical pearl: A positive rapid test in low-prevalence setting needs confirmation
slides.highlight: PPV and NPV are NOT fixed properties; they strictly depend on disease prevalence

slides.title: Worked Example: Rapid Strep Test
slides.subtitle: 1,000 children with pharyngitis, 20% prevalence (200 true cases)
points: Test has 90% sensitivity (180 TP, 20 FN) and 90% specificity (720 TN, 80 FP)
Sensitivity: 180 / 200 = 90% | Specificity: 720 / 800 = 90%
slides.highlight: Exam trap: Despite 90% spec, ~3 in 10 positive tests here are false positives!

slides.title: Intrinsic vs Extrinsic Metrics
slides.subtitle: Sens & Spec || PPV & NPV
points: Column-wise calculations || Row-wise calculations
Independent of prevalence || Highly dependent on prevalence
Evaluates the test tool || Guides bedside clinical decision
Formula: a/(a+c) and d/(b+d) || Formula: a/(a+b) and d/(c+d)
slides.highlight: Likelihood ratios (LR+ = Sens/(1-Spec)) combine both and remain prevalence-independent

slides.title: Viva Cheat Sheet
slides.subtitle: Quick recall for the biostatistics station
points: Screening tests demand high sensitivity (do not miss cases, e.g., newborn TSH)
Confirmatory tests demand high specificity (avoid false labels, e.g., sweat chloride in CF)
Post-test odds = Pre-test odds × Likelihood Ratio (convert probability to odds first)
slides.highlight: Exam pearl: When prevalence is low, even an accurate test yields low PPV

caption:
Biostatistics stations in MD/DNB pediatric practicals can make or break your score.

Examiners love asking: 'If a test is 95% sensitive and 95% specific, does a positive result mean the child has a 95% chance of having the disease?'

The answer is a resounding NO—because PPV strictly depends on the prevalence of the disease in your clinical setting.

Swipe through for the classic 2x2 setup, SnNOut/SpPIn rules, and a fully worked numerical example.

What biostatistics topic trips you up the most: Odds Ratio or ROC curves?

Save 🔖 & share with a batchmate.

For education only; follow local protocols.
references: Gordis Epidemiology, 6th Edition (Chapter 5: Assessing the Validity and Reliability of Diagnostic and Screening Tests)
doctor_check: Slide 7: Corrected formula from 'Post-test probability' to 'Post-test odds = Pre-test odds × Likelihood Ratio', as probability cannot be multiplied directly by LR without converting to odds.
Slide 7: Replaced outdated 'HIV Western blot' example with 'sweat chloride in CF' (Western blot is superseded by HIV-1/2 differentiation assays and NAT/PCR in modern pediatric algorithms).
Slide 5: Harmonized the false-positive proportion wording between point 3 and the highlight box (~3 in 10, since 80/260 = 30.8%).
References: Removed unverified parenthetical chapter title from Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics.
